![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14196324/assets/e77723ba949432ad0ec57cb848b6b3e0a84fb03c1f0b6bdd653606a85afedaba.png)

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius $2.5,$ as shown above. Find the maximum possible area of the triangle.
question.worked_solution:
Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{25-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{25-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $5$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<5.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{25-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{25-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{25-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{25-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ 25-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ {l}^{2} & =\frac{25}{2} \\ l & =\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}$ | $(\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2},5)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $4$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Finally, the maximum possible area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A(\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{25-{(\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
